title: Public demand for economic-system change is broad, but the social contract is weakened by distrust that governments can deliver long-term benefits
source_unit: Earth4All, Rebuild Trust: Rigged economies, fractured societies and the case for change, Earth for All Survey 2026, conducted by Ipsos
geography: 17 countries representing 58% of global GDP, 38% of world population, and 37% of fossil-fuel and industrial CO2 emissions; G20 countries surveyed except China, Russia, and Saudi Arabia, plus Sweden

observations.period: February-March 2026; perceived economic fairness and demand for system change

too_much_inequality.unit: percent agreeing there is too much economic inequality in their country

rigged_system.unit: percent agreeing the economic system is rigged to benefit the rich and powerful

major_change.unit: percent wanting major changes to the economic system

opposition_to_change.unit: percent disagreeing that major economic change is needed

observations.method: Ipsos survey conducted for Earth4All between 20 February and 6 March 2026, with national data weighted by age, gender, region, and working status; countries excluded for political sensitivities are documented in the report.
observations.uncertainty: These are cross-national perceptions and stated preferences, not measures of objective inequality, a representative global population, policy feasibility, or support for one specific reform package.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 17 large economies, with country, income, status, political, and demographic differences analyzed in the report.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broad agreement that the system is unfair can support different and conflicting reforms; demand for change does not establish a shared diagnosis of causes or remedies.

observations.period: 2026; long-term government trust and perceived social division

long_term_government_trust.unit: percent believing their government will make decisions benefiting the majority 20 or 30 years from now

greater_division.unit: percent saying their country is more divided than a decade ago

political_tension.unit: percent perceiving serious tension between supporters of different political parties

income_tension.unit: percent perceiving serious tension between high- and low-income people

social_contract_route.value: public support for transformation is separated from confidence that institutions can deliver it over time

observations.method: Cross-national survey comparison of perceived division, group tension, and long-term confidence in government; the report frames these as components of the social contract.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived division and long-term trust are not direct measures of institutional performance, social interaction, policy delivery, or future political behavior.
observations.subgroup: Adults across political, income, immigrant/native-born, climate-attitude, and national contexts represented in the survey.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low long-term confidence can coexist with effective short-term government action, local trust, civic cooperation, or future institutional repair.

democracy_best.unit: percent saying democracy is the best way to govern their country

unconstrained_strong_leader.unit: percent saying their country would be better off with a strong leader unconstrained by parliament and elections

legitimacy_tension.value: support for democracy in principle coexists with willingness to trade institutional constraints for decisive leadership

observations.method: Ipsos cross-national survey with direct questions on preferred governing system and unconstrained-leader alternatives.
observations.uncertainty: Abstract regime preferences do not predict voting, authoritarian behavior, policy outcomes, or willingness to abandon democratic safeguards in a concrete political crisis.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 17 countries, with stronger unconstrained-leader preference reported in several upper-middle-income countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Preference for decisive leadership may express frustration with institutional deadlock rather than rejection of elections, rights, or accountability.

strong_climate_action.unit: percent accepting strong government emissions action even at the cost of higher prices

conditional_support.value: support falls among lower-income, lower-status, and right-leaning respondents and is higher in lower- and upper-middle-income countries than in high-income countries

delivery_condition.value: public consent for long-horizon transformation depends on whether near-term costs are seen as fairly distributed and institutions as acting for the majority

observations.method: Survey questions on emissions policy, price trade-offs, and social-position differences, interpreted alongside the report's social-contract framework.
observations.uncertainty: Stated climate-policy support is not a forecast of actual consumption, voting, protest, compliance, or emissions outcomes; subgroup differences may reflect multiple correlated factors.
observations.subgroup: Respondents differentiated by income, perceived social status, political orientation, and national income context.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support may increase when policy design provides visible benefits, compensation, participation, or credible enforcement even if price effects remain.

related_sources.claim: Club of Rome publication page summarizing the Earth for All Survey 2026.
Official 61-page Earth for All Survey 2026 report with methodology and country summaries.

boundary: This record adds a social-contract route from perceived inequality and demand for economic-system change through long-term government trust, perceived social division, democratic legitimacy, and consent for climate transformation. It is a weighted cross-national public-opinion study, not an objective inequality estimate, causal test of trust, forecast of political regime change, or respondent-level life-history dataset.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Club of Rome publication page and Earth4All PDF reviewed for sample frame, field dates, economic-system perceptions, long-term government trust, social division, democratic preferences, and climate-policy cost trade-offs.
